title: Jeppesen ForeFlight's Device-as-a-Service EFB Model Is a Bet That Airline Procurement, Not Features, Is the Real Bottleneck
summary: Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix's Manage My EFB bundles hardware, software, and lifecycle services into a single subscription — reframing EFB fleet management as a procurement and total-cost problem, not just a technology decision.
body_markdown:
The dominant conversation about EFB platform competition has always centered on features: which platform has better weather integration, smarter NOTAM filtering, tighter flight planning workflows. That framing isn't wrong, but it misses a layer of friction that airline EFB program managers quietly deal with every day — and that's the part Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix are targeting with their newly launched Manage My EFB offering.

## What the Product Actually Is

<cite index="10-2,10-3">Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix Corporation announced the launch of Manage My EFB in June, positioning it as a comprehensive Device-as-a-Service solution designed to simplify and scale EFB programs for commercial aviation operators. The offering introduces a subscription-based delivery model that bundles devices, Jeppesen ForeFlight EFB software, Stratix lifecycle services, and connectivity into a single, predictable cost per device, per month.</cite> It's available exclusively through Jeppesen ForeFlight, which means the commercial relationship stays with the EFB software vendor rather than splitting across multiple procurement channels.

<cite index="13-4">Jeppesen delivers the EFB platform itself while Stratix manages the full device lifecycle — including Apple iPad hardware, connectivity, support, and visibility — all within one predictable subscription.</cite> That bundling is the core strategic move here. What looks like a mobility services deal is actually a bet about where EFB buying decisions get stuck.

## The Procurement Problem Is Bigger Than It Looks

Anyone who's been involved in deploying EFB software at scale knows that the software evaluation is often the easy part. The harder questions involve device procurement timelines, MDM configuration, Apple Business Manager enrollment, connectivity SLAs, device replacement logistics for distributed fleets, and what happens when a pilot's iPad fails on a layover in a city where no one from IT is reachable. Those problems don't show up in feature comparison matrices, but they consume a meaningful amount of program manager time.

Manage My EFB is essentially arguing that collapsing all of that into a single vendor relationship — and a single line item on a budget — is worth something to airlines. <cite index="13-8">Stratix's own framing of this, as quoted in the announcement, is that "airlines are looking for ways to simplify operations while maintaining the highest levels of reliability and compliance."</cite> That's corporate-speak for a real operational tension: the pressure to reduce vendor complexity without sacrificing the control that airlines need for regulatory compliance on EFB configurations.

The "per device, per month" model also carries a subtler commercial implication. It converts what was previously a lumpy capital expenditure cycle — hardware refreshes every three to four years, large upfront software licensing — into a flatter operating expense. For airlines managing tight cost structures, that predictability has genuine appeal, and it lowers the barrier to fleet-wide EFB standardization for carriers that might have been running a patchwork of device generations.

## What This Means Competitively

The strategic signal here is that Jeppesen ForeFlight is expanding its surface area in the EFB relationship beyond the software subscription. By tying device lifecycle management into its commercial offering, it makes switching more friction-laden for an airline that has committed to the bundle. That's not a criticism — it's a rational platform play, and it mirrors what enterprise software vendors in other industries figured out years ago: the stickiest customer relationships are the ones where you own more of the operational dependency stack.

The open question is whether airlines will actually want a single vendor holding the keys to both the software and the hardware lifecycle, or whether procurement teams will prefer to keep those relationships separate for negotiating leverage. EFB software decisions typically sit with flight operations, while device and MDM management often involves IT procurement — and the two groups don't always agree on what "simplified" means.

The timing of this launch, against a backdrop of rising AI feature velocity in the EFB market (as I've covered in previous posts about ForeFlight's ClearNotams rollout and the broader push from Aviobook and Adventure Pilot), suggests that incumbents are increasingly competing on the total program relationship, not just the software stack. Whether a Device-as-a-Service model proves durable as an EFB differentiator probably depends less on the concept itself and more on whether Stratix's execution at airline scale holds up in practice.

The 'per device, per month' model converts hardware from capex to opex for airlines. In your experience working EFB deals, was procurement structure — capex vs. opex — ever actually a decision-driver at the airline level, or does that distinction mostly matter at the CFO layer and rarely change what flight ops recommends? (Yes, it's a real driver / Rarely changes the recommendation / Depends on the airline type.)

The stickiest risk in a bundle like this is execution: if Stratix's device logistics fail on a layover, it reflects on ForeFlight. Is that kind of reputational co-dependency a reason to stay separate, or is it the normal trade-off of any deep partnership in aviation tech?
email_brief: Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix launched 'Manage My EFB' in June 2026 — a Device-as-a-Service bundle that rolls EFB software, Apple iPad hardware, MDM/lifecycle management, and connectivity into a single per-device monthly subscription for commercial airlines. The story fits squarely into a broader trend of EFB vendors expanding their competitive surface area beyond the software layer itself, using total program ownership as a retention and growth strategy. It's relevant right now because AI feature velocity in the EFB market is rising fast (ForeFlight's own ClearNotams launch, Aviobook's Meteomatics integration), and incumbents appear to be responding by making the overall EFB program relationship stickier — not just the software. The commercial question is whether airlines will accept a single-vendor dependency across both software and hardware, or whether they'll push back to preserve procurement leverage.
